introduction.text: Castel Sant'Angelo, also known as the Mausoleum of Hadrian, is a towering cylindrical building in Rome, Italy. It was initially commissioned by the Roman Emperor Hadrian as a mausoleum for himself and his family, later served as a papal fortress and castle, and is now a museum. It was once the tallest building in Rome.

history.description: The tomb of Roman Emperor Hadrian, also called Hadrian's mole, was erected on the right bank of the Tiber between 134 and 139 AD.
Hadrian's ashes were placed here in 138 AD, along with those of his wife Sabina and his first adopted son, Lucius Aelius, who also died in 138 AD.
The remains of succeeding emperors were also interred here, with the last recorded deposition being Caracalla in 217 AD.
The building was converted into a military fortress in 401 AD and subsequently included in the Aurelian Walls by Flavius Honorius Augustus.
Visigoth looters scattered the urns and ashes during Alaric's sacking of Rome in 410 AD.
Original decorative bronze and stone statuary was thrown down upon attacking Goths when they besieged Rome in 537 AD, as recounted by Procopius.

Legend states that the Archangel Michael appeared atop the mausoleum in 590 AD, sheathing his sword as a sign of the end of a plague, thus giving the castle its present name. Pope Gregory I also had a vision of an angel atop the castle.
Popes began converting the structure into a castle during the 14th century.
Pope Clement VII took refuge in the fortress from the siege of Charles V's Landsknechte during the Sack of Rome in 1527.

In 1676, Cornelis de Bruijn noted a custom where, upon a pope's death like Pope Clement X, all prisoners with heavy sentences were moved to Sant'Angelo, and then all other prisoners in Rome were released except those in Sant'Angelo.
Cornelis de Bruijn also mentioned an annual fireworks display at the castle on St. Peter's Day, which he observed in 1676.
The castle was decommissioned in 1901 and is now a museum, the Museo Nazionale di Castel Sant'Angelo.
Pope Nicholas III connected the castle to St Peter's Basilica by a covered fortified corridor called the Passetto di Borgo.
The Papal State used Sant'Angelo as a prison for notable figures such as Giordano Bruno, Benvenuto Cellini, and Cagliostro, with executions performed in the small inner courtyard.
Giorgio Vasari noted in the 16th century that stone columns from Hadrian's tomb were taken to decorate Saint Peter's Basilica.
An ongoing project aims to connect Castel Sant'Angelo to St. Peter's Basilica via a fully pedestrian path, by creating an underground tunnel.

design.description: Originally, the mausoleum was a decorated cylinder with a garden top and a golden quadriga.
Emperor Hadrian also built the Pons Aelius bridge, which still provides a scenic approach from the center of Rome and features Baroque additions of statues of angels.

art.description: Pope Leo X built a chapel within the castle that featured a Madonna by Raffaello da Montelupo.
In 1536, Raffaello da Montelupo created a marble statue of Saint Michael holding his sword to surmount the Castel.

In 1753, Peter Anton von Verschaffelt created a bronze statue of Saint Michael to replace Montelupo's on the castle's summit; Montelupo's original statue can now be seen in an open court inside the castle.
The castle served as the setting for the third act of Giacomo Puccini's 1900 opera Tosca.
